title: Vayikra: when a leader errs (Leviticus 4:22)
hook: the text says "when", not "if"; leaders will make mistakes
tomorrow: Tzav: the fire shall not go out

segments.voice: Yesterday, salt on every offering and on the Friday night bread. Your line was salt of the covenant. What promise did you remember? Day three hundred eighty-four.

When did you last hear a leader admit a mistake in public? A boss, a principal, a mayor, a coach. Not a vague we regret any confusion, but a plain I got that wrong. It's rare enough that people remember it. Chapter four of Leviticus is a list of offerings for mistakes, the kind made without meaning to. It goes through four kinds of people, from the high priest down to an ordinary individual. Three of them are introduced with the word if. One is introduced with a different word. He's the leader.
screen: `I GOT THAT WRONG.` → `OFFERINGS FOR MISTAKES.` → `THREE IFS, ONE DIFFERENT WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the list. If the anointed priest sins. If the whole congregation errs. If any one of the common people sins. And in between, in the JPS 1917 translation: "When a ruler sinneth." The Hebrew there is asher, when, instead of im, if. The ruler, the nasi, is a tribal chief or a king, someone with real power. And the Torah doesn't say if he makes a mistake. It says when. These are errors made without intent, the Hebrew calls it shegagah, an honest slip. And for a person in charge, the text seems to assume they will happen. Commentators heard two things in that small word. Some read it as a warning: power makes mistakes almost certain. The more decisions you make, the more people you affect, the more often you'll be wrong. Rashi hears something hopeful. He cites the Talmud, which plays on the sound of asher and hears ashrei, happy. Happy is the generation whose leader brings an offering for his mistakes. If he admits the ones he made without meaning to, the Talmud says, how much more will he regret the ones he made on purpose. So the leader isn't excused, and he isn't condemned for being human. He's expected to own it, publicly, by walking up to the altar with everyone watching. A leader who never makes mistakes isn't in the Torah's picture at all. A leader who admits them is a gift to the whole generation.
screen: `IF, IF, IF, AND THEN: WHEN.` · `SHEGAGAH: AN HONEST SLIP.` · `POWER MAKES MISTAKES LIKELY.` · `ASHREI: HAPPY THE GENERATION.` · then, large: `WHEN, NOT IF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive a leader's honest mistake. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone with responsibility over you, at work, at school, in your family, in your community, who got something wrong without meaning to. Notice whatever you still carry about it. Then try seeing it the way the Torah does: of course they made a mistake; they're a leader. And if you're the one in charge somewhere, think of one slip of your own you could admit plainly. The bell holds the time.
Vayikra. And He called. The book that says when a ruler errs, not if, and asks the leader to own it in public.
Your line: when, not if. Today, if you make an honest mistake, say so plainly, the first time, without a long excuse. Day three hundred eighty-four.

screen: `DAY 384 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TZAV: THE FIRE SHALL NOT GO OUT.`

howItsDone: Jewish teaching often cites the Talmud's 'happy is the generation whose leader brings an offering for his mistakes' when speaking about leaders acknowledging error.

myth: the Torah says 'if a ruler sins'
it says when: asher, not im.
Leviticus 4 is about mistakes made without intent
the Talmud hears ashrei, happy, in the word for when
happy is the generation whose leader brings an offering for his mistakes.

fork.setup: you're a tribal chief, and you've realized you broke a law without meaning to. the whole camp will see if you bring an offering. what does the Torah expect?
options: keep quiet: a leader can't look weak.
bring the offering and own the mistake.
have someone else bring it for you.
fork.reveal: he brings his own offering. and the Talmud says: happy is the generation whose leader does that.

original.note: Hebrew: when a ruler sins, Leviticus 4:22.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule about sacrifices for sins.
what it means: the Torah expects leaders to make honest mistakes, and to own them in public.
what a scholar hears: the verse switches from im (if) to asher (when) for the nasi; Rashi, following Horayot 10b, reads asher as ashrei: happy the generation whose leader atones for his errors.

sources.ref: Rashi on Leviticus 4:22; Babylonian Talmud, Horayot 10b

notes: Audit (10% sample): hook no longer opens with the templated 'Think of...'.
